work_or_object: Wilhelm Schmitz, Commentarii Notarum Tironianarum, especially Tabula 32
evidence_used: Actual note tables and the fifteen attested derivational/compound families used in the crosswalk
limitations: Edition is modern and underlying practice is early medieval, not ca.1420

work_or_object: Martin Hellmann, Supertextus Notarum Tironianarum: basis, structure, word notes and terminations
dating: Digital project based on CNT and manuscript work
evidence_used: Explicit separation of basic word notes from syllable/ending notes; line/element construction; TINCT family and searchable forms
limitations: Digital lexicon is a modern access instrument, not a late-medieval manual

work_or_object: Martin Hellmann, Geschichte / Vorgeschichte of the Tironian lexicon
evidence_used: Carolingian revival and chancery/school use; notes become rare by the 10th century; later appearances reflect individual antiquarian interest
limitations: Concise synthesis rather than full monograph

work_or_object: A. C. Dionisotti ed., Expositio Notarum, introduction
evidence_used: CNT has about 13000 word-note pairs; ordering by analyzable basic elements and topics; explicit DIVES family
limitations: Only the publisher excerpt was available

work_or_object: Christoph Walther, Tironian Notes and Legal Practice
repository_or_publisher: De Gruyter, New Approaches to Shorthand
evidence_used: Distinction between rote use of individual signs and comprehensive sentence-level competence; mixed shorthand/longhand legal use

work_or_object: Paris BnF Latin 8779 and other Commentarii witnesses
evidence_used: Digital primary-witness inventory and IIIF access for the CNT tradition

work_or_object: Cod. Guelf. 9.8 Aug. 4°, Commentarii notarum tironiarum
evidence_used: Dated digitized manuscript description: Tironian notes paired with Carolingian minuscule, two hands

work_or_object: John Haines, Did John of Tilbury write an Ars notaria?
dating: 2008 study; manuscripts second half 13th c., ca.1300, 14th c.
evidence_used: Detailed reconstruction of the Ars notoria scribendi, its 19 minim-derived shapes, claimed two/three-stroke word encoding, internal contradictions, manuscript dates and non-Tilbury authorship
limitations: OCR is imperfect; conclusions checked against article pagination and quoted Latin

work_or_object: John Haines, The Notory Art of Shorthand (Ars notoria notarie)
evidence_used: Confirms critical edition and English translation of the unique hybrid shorthand/hermetic treatise
limitations: Publisher description, not a substitute for the critical edition

work_or_object: Universitat de Barcelona UBTERM, notae iuris
dating: Modern reference; phenomenon known from 3rd c. onward
evidence_used: Notae iuris combine simple/syllabic suspension, contraction, Tironian-derived abbreviations and conventional signs; examples c'=cum, p with superscript s=post, bfio=beneficio, oia=omnia, p variants=per/pro
limitations: Short terminology entry; does not demonstrate a unified 1420 code

evidence_used: Four main abbreviation mechanisms; doubling for plural; nasal and er marks; memorized measures/currency units; explicit warning that medieval practice was not uniform
limitations: Teaching guide rather than corpus edition
